# Abstract
We present a general model for accelerated radiometric decay that can be used to estimate the equivalent young-earth ages of rocks and geologic horizons given a secular age . 
The model is based on specifying a time-deependent decay rate $\lambda(t)$ as a piecewise function that defines how the rate of radiometric decay evolves through time, with parameters that can be specified or solved for given appropriate data. 
The model assumes two possible periods of accelerated decay, one during the Creation week and one during the Flood, with the decay rate decaying back to the background rate after each period.
Following the initial acceleration, $\lambda(t)$ decays back to the background decay rate $\lambda_{bg}$ as an exponential function of time, with decay constant $k_c$ and $k_F$ for the post-Creation week and post-Flood periods, respectively.
By specifying pairs of matched dates (young-earth and secular), it is possible to calibrate the model to estimate the model parameters, which then allows it to be used for age estimation.
Using this approach, we can build a numerical solver for mathmetically calculating a young-earth age given a secular age, and vice versa.
In this paper, we derive the general model and provide examples of calibrated age relationships based on various hypothesized matched date pairs. 
The predictions from these example models can then be used to calculate various parameters of relevance to young-earth creation studies, for example, the rates of sediment flux and mountain building during the Flood, the timing of the end of the Flood with regards to the geologic period, and the point at which the accelerated decay rates return to the background rate.
The framework we propose is very flexible and can be used to explore the implications of accelerated decay for various creation issues.

```{python}
#| label: setup

# Every date, age and model evaluation in this paper comes from the `card`
# package, so the paper and the code cannot drift apart.  The naming rule is
# that a DATE counts years after Day 1 of Creation and an AGE counts years
# before present; the two run in opposite directions and sum to AGE_OF_EARTH.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from card import (
    AGE_OF_EARTH,        # AGE of Day 1 of Creation (and DATE of the present)
    DEFAULT_CHRONOLOGY,  # the chronology every constant below is derived from
    FLOOD_AGE,           # AGE at which the Flood begins
    FLOOD_START_DATE,    # DATE at which the Flood begins
    ICE_AGE_END_AGE,     # AGE at which the Ice Age ends
    GeneralModel,
    GeneralModelParams,
)
```

## General Model Derivation

In order to develop the general model, we make a series of assumptions that limit the mathematical form of the time-dependent decay rate, $\lambda(t)$. 
First, we assume that there are two periods of accelerated decay, one during the Creation week and one during the Flood. 
These periods of accelerated decay are assumed to be followed by a period of exponential decay back to the background decay rate, $\lambda_{bg}$, which is the decay rate measured today.
Accelerated decay may occur instantaneously at the start of the Creation week and the Flood and then immediately begin to decline, or there may be an extended time period over which the decay rate returns to the background, depending on the decay constant, which can be specified separately for each accelerated period.
Finally, we assume that all different isotopes are affected percentage-wise the same, so that the ratio of decay rates for any isotope to the background decay rate is the same for all isotopes.b 
This essentially means that we do not directly model the decay of any particular isotope, but instead we model the geologic time scale directly. 

With these assumptions, we can define a general mathematical framework for the time-dependent decay rate, $\lambda(t)$, as a piecewise function that defines how the rate of radiometric decay evolves through time.

The basic model is as follows: 
$$
\lambda(t) = \begin{cases}
\lambda_c &  0 < t < t_c \\
\left(\lambda_c - \lambda_{bg}\right) e^{-k_c (t - t_c)} + \lambda_{bg} & t_c < t \leq t_{F} \\
\lambda_F & t_{F} < t < t_{F2} \\
\left(\lambda_F - \lambda_{bg}\right) e^{-k_F (t - t_{F2})} + \lambda_{bg} & t_{F2} < t \\
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-general-model}

where $t$ is the time in years after Day 1 of creation, denoted as $t_0$. 
We can plot the general mathematical model represented in @eq-general-model using Python: 

```{python}
#| label: fig-general-model
#| fig-cap: "Schematic diagram of the general model showing model behavior. "
# lambda(t) comes straight from the package, so this figure always shows the
# same function the solver integrates.  A one-year Flood is used here purely so
# that the third region is visible; the flood-only limit sets t_F2 == t_F.
schematic = GeneralModel(GeneralModelParams(
    lambda_c=1e3,
    lambda_F=1e5,
    lambda_bg=1.0,
    k_c=1e-1,
    k_F=1e-2,
    t_c=1,
    t_F=FLOOD_START_DATE,
    t_F2=FLOOD_START_DATE + 1,
))

ts = np.linspace(0, AGE_OF_EARTH, 1000)
rates = np.array([schematic.lambda_func(t) for t in ts])

plt.semilogy(ts, rates)
plt.xlabel('Time (years after Creation)')
plt.ylabel(r'$\lambda(t)/\lambda_{bg}$')
plt.title('Generalized Radiometric Decay Model')
plt.grid()
plt.show()
```

@fig-general-model shows schematically how @eq-general-model would look for a particular set of choices for the parameters. 
This model has a total of 7 parameters that can either be specified or solved for, given appropriate data.

- $\lambda_{bg}$: the background decay rate, what is measured today. To make things simpler, we normalize $\lambda(t)$ by $\lambda_{bg}$, so that $\lambda_{bg} = 1$ and all other decay rates are expressed as a ratio to the background decay rate. This works because of our assumption that all isotopes are affected percentage-wise the same, so that the ratio of decay rates for any isotope to the background decay rate is the same for all isotopes.
- $t_c$: Day 7 of Creation Week, an unknown number of years before present (YBP). Note that $t$ (time in years after creation) is related to YBP as $t = t_p - \text{YBP}$, where $t_p$ is the present in years after Day 1 of creation. @eq-general-model can be re-written using this to put everything in terms of YBP if desired. 
- $t_{F}$: the start time of accelerated decay during the Flood
- $t_{F2}$: the end time of accelerated decay during the Flood
- $\lambda_c$: the decay rate ($\lambda(t)$) _during_ the creation week, which equal to or greater than the background
- $\lambda_F$: the decay rate ($\lambda(t)$) _during_ the Flood, which is equal to or greater than the background
- $k_c$: the decay constant for the decay rate of $\lambda(t)$ following the Creation week and prior to the Flood, during the post-creation period
- $k_F$: the decay constant for the decay rate of $\lambda(t)$ following the Flood, during the post-Flood period

There are other models that would be more general extensions of this model, for example, we could have a ramp-up of accelerated decay rates or non-constant decay rates during the Creation week or the Flood, but this model is a good starting point for understanding the general behavior of the system and how it can be used to make predictions and test hypotheses.

From this general model various simplifications can be derived. 
For example, one simplification is to assume that $t_{F} = t_{F2}$ (i.e., peak accelerated decay is instantaneous and $\lambda(t)$ immediately starts to decay back to $\lambda_{bg}$), and that $\lambda_c = \lambda_{bg}$, which would imply no acceleration of decay during the Creation week. 
In this scenario, $\lambda(t)$ is simply the background rate until the start of the Flood, at which time it jumps up instantaneously and then decays back to the background rate over some period of time.
Under this assumption, @eq-general-model-YBP becomes:
$$
\lambda(t) = \begin{cases}
\left(\lambda_F - \lambda_{bg}\right) e^{k_F (\tau - t_{F})} + \lambda_{bg} & \tau \le t_{F} \\
\lambda_{bg} &  \tau > t_F \\
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-flood-only-model} 


Now consider the differential equation for radiometric decay, which is given by:
$$
\frac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda(t) N
$$ {#eq-decay-rate-differential}
Note that here we have switched to $t$ again to denote that this is forward time. 
This can be solved to give the number of atoms remaining as a function of time:
$$
N(t) = N_0 e^{-\int_{t_f}^{t_p} \lambda(t') dt'}
$$ {#eq-decay-rate-integral}
where $N_0$ is the initial number of atoms and $\lambda(t)$ is the  time-dependent decay rate given by @eq-general-model **[cite Mogk here]**. 
$t_f$ is the time of formation of the rock, and $t_p$ is the present, both in years after Day 1 of creation.
$t'$ here is the integration variable. 
The ratio of remaining to original atoms is given by:
$$
r(t) = \frac{N(t)}{N_0} = e^{-\int_{t_f}^{t_p} \lambda(t') dt'}
$$ {#eq-ratio-integral}
In the secular model, where $\lambda$ is constant and equal to $\lambda_{bg}$, this simplifies to:
$$
r(t_{sec}) = e^{-\lambda_{bg} t_{sec}}
$$ {#eq-ratio-secular}
In the young-age model, where $\lambda$ is a function of time, we have:
$$
r(t_p) = e^{-\int_{t_f}^{t_p} \lambda(t') dt'}
$$ {#eq-ratio-young-age}
where 0 is the time of formation of the rock and $t_p$ is the present in years after Day 1 of creation.

We can run experiments by considering cases where the ages of a rock or geologic horizon within the two models is known. 
The ratio of daughter to parent products is the same for both the secular and young-age models while the ages are different. 
Thus, we can set the ratios for the two models equal to each other and take the logarithm of both sides, normalizing by the background decay rate to get:
$$
t_{sec} = \int_{t_f}^{t_p} \frac{\lambda(t')}{\lambda_{bg}} dt'
$$ 
where we need to substitute the appropriate time-dependence for $\lambda(t)$ from @eq-general-model. 
Since @eq-general-model is a piecewise function, we evaluate the integral piecewise as well. 
<!-- However, we need to now consider a change of variables to express the integral in terms of YBP, in order to make use of @eq-flood-only-model.  -->

<!-- To relate $t$ to $\tau$, we can use the relationship $t = t_p - \tau$, where $t_p$ is the present in years after Day 1 of creation.
For the integration then, $dt = -d\tau$, the limits of integration change from $t=0$ and $t=t_p$ to $\tau = t_{ya}$ and $\tau = 0$.
Flipping the limits of integration (note that the two negative signs cancel) gives: -->
$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{sec} & = \int_{t_f}^{t_p} \frac{\lambda(\tau)}{\lambda_{bg}} d\tau\\
& = \left(\frac{\lambda_F - \lambda_{bg}}{\lambda_{bg}}\right) \int_{t_{limit}}^{t_{p}}  e^{-k_F \tau} d\tau + \int_{t_f}^{t_{F}} d\tau + \int_{t_F}^{t_p} d\tau \\
& = A_{ya} + R \int_{t_{limit}}^{t_{p}}  e^{-k_F \tau} d\tau \\
& = A_{ya} + \frac{R}{k_F} \left(e^{-k_F t_{limit}} - e^{-k_F t_{p}}  \right) \\
& = A_{ya} + \frac{R}{k_F} \left(e^{-k_F (A_E - A_{ya})} - e^{-k_F A_E}  \right) \\
& = A_{ya} + \frac{R}{k_F} e^{-k_F A_E} \left(e^{k_F A_{ya}} - 1  \right) \\
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-integral-flood-only-1}
where $t_{limit} = t_F$ if $t_f \le t_F$ and $t_{limit} = t_f$ if $t_{f} > t_F$. 
$R = (\lambda_F - \lambda_{bg})/ \lambda_{bg}$ is the normalized ratio of the flood decay rate $\lambda_F$ to the background decay rate.
<!-- If $t_{ya} < t_F$, then we simply integrate to $t_{ya}$ instead of $t_F$ in the first integral. -->

Using @eq-integral-flood-only-1, we can test several hypotheses. 
For example, given two pairs of ages known in both the secular and young-age models, we can calculate the decay constant $k_F$ and decay rate ratio $R$. 
As an example, let us consider the start of the Flood.
Assume the Flood begins at the Precambrian-Cambrian boundary, an event dated on the secular time-scale to be ~540 Ma.
Take the end of the Ice Age as another data point, conventionally dated to be around 11.7 ka.
The matching young-age estimates are read from the chronology configuration rather than written in by hand, so that changing the assumed chronology updates every number that follows:

```{python}
#| label: constraints
#| code-summary: "The two matched date pairs"
FLOOD_SECULAR = 541e6     # Precambrian-Cambrian boundary, secular age (years)
ICE_AGE_SECULAR = 11.7e3  # end of the Ice Age, secular age (years)

print(f"Age of the Earth   A_E  = {AGE_OF_EARTH:,.0f} YBP")
print(f"Flood begins       A_F  = {FLOOD_AGE:,.0f} YBP  (secular {FLOOD_SECULAR:.3g} yr)")
print(f"Ice Age ends       A_IA = {ICE_AGE_END_AGE:,.0f} YBP  (secular {ICE_AGE_SECULAR:.4g} yr)")
```

Writing $A_F$ and $A_{IA}$ for these two young ages, $A_{sec,F}$ and $A_{sec,IA}$ for their secular counterparts, and $A_E$ for the age of the Earth, substituting into @eq-integral-flood-only-1 gives:
$$
A_{sec,F} - A_F = \frac{R}{k_F} e^{-k_F A_E} \left(e^{k_F A_F} - 1\right)
$$ {#eq-flood-constraint}

and
$$
A_{sec,IA} - A_{IA} = \frac{R}{k_F} e^{-k_F A_E} \left(e^{k_F A_{IA}} - 1\right)
$$ {#eq-iceAge-constraint}


@eq-constraint-ratio has no closed-form solution for $k_F$, but its right-hand side is monotonic in $k_F$, so the root is unique and is found immediately by bisection; $R$ then follows from either constraint.
Rather than approximate this by hand, we solve the two constraints directly against the model, which avoids relying on the large-$k_F$ approximations that @eq-constraint-ratio would otherwise require:

```{python}
#| label: calibration
#| code-summary: "Solve the two constraints for lambda_F and k_F"
from scipy.optimize import fsolve

flood_date = DEFAULT_CHRONOLOGY.flood_start_date

def residuals(theta):
    """Log-space misfit of both matched date pairs, evaluated on the model."""
    model = GeneralModel.flood_only(lambda_F=10 ** theta[0],
                                    k_F=10 ** theta[1],
                                    t_F=flood_date)
    return [np.log10(model.forward_age(FLOOD_AGE) / FLOOD_SECULAR),
            np.log10(model.forward_age(ICE_AGE_END_AGE) / ICE_AGE_SECULAR)]

log_lambda_F, log_k_F = fsolve(residuals, [6.5, -2.3])
lambda_F, k_F = 10 ** log_lambda_F, 10 ** log_k_F
R = lambda_F - 1
calibrated = GeneralModel.flood_only(lambda_F=lambda_F, k_F=k_F, t_F=flood_date)

print(f"lambda_F = {lambda_F:,.0f} x background   (R = {R:,.0f})")
print(f"k_F      = {k_F:.4g} / year")
print()
print(f"check  Flood   {FLOOD_AGE:,.0f} YBP -> "
      f"{calibrated.forward_age(FLOOD_AGE):.4g} yr  (target {FLOOD_SECULAR:.4g})")
print(f"check  Ice Age {ICE_AGE_END_AGE:,.0f} YBP -> "
      f"{calibrated.forward_age(ICE_AGE_END_AGE):.4g} yr  (target {ICE_AGE_SECULAR:.4g})")
```

Both constraints are honored exactly, which is expected: two free parameters fitted to two matched date pairs.

It is important to note that this derivation made several assumptions about the timing and dates of the beginning of the Flood and the Ice Age in the rock record, which could be debated. 
Other comparative dates for these events could easily be substituted for the ones used here, and the resulting parameters would be slightly different. 
The point is that this is a completely generalizable model for which, given any constraints or assumptions about the timing of these events, we can derive the equivalent decay rates within a young-age framework. 

With this framework, we now can not only make predictions, but test those predictions against observations. 

# Discussion

## Discussion Point 1

```{python}
#| label: fig-age-curve
#| fig-cap: "Secular age as a function of young age under the calibrated flood-only model."
#| code-summary: "Forward age curve and the inverse of a given secular age"
# forward_age is the package's exact evaluation of @eq-integral-flood-only-1,
# so this curve is the model itself rather than a re-derivation of it.
t_sec = 65e6  # 65 million years in the secular model

young_ages = np.linspace(0, AGE_OF_EARTH, 1000)
secular_ages = np.array([calibrated.forward_age(a) for a in young_ages])

plt.semilogy(young_ages, secular_ages)
plt.semilogy([0, young_ages[-1]], [t_sec, t_sec], 'r--')
plt.axvline(FLOOD_AGE, color='0.6', linestyle=':')
plt.xlabel('Young age (years before present)')
plt.ylabel('Secular age (years)')
plt.title('Young-age equivalent of secular ages under the flood-only model')
plt.grid()
plt.show()

print(f"Ratio of flood decay rate to background decay rate: {lambda_F:,.0f}")
print(f"A rock dated to {t_sec:.3g} secular years formed "
      f"{calibrated.inverse_age(t_sec):,.0f} years before present.")
print(f"Oldest secular age this model can produce: "
      f"{calibrated.forward_age(AGE_OF_EARTH):.4g} years.")
```
